title: 175 Salt-limited trace mineral and/or protein supplement intake behavior and subsequent performance of yearling heifers grazing summer/early fall dryland pastures
content:
Abstract
A study was conducted at Fort Ellis Experiment Station in Bozeman, Montana (MAES) to evaluate supplement intake behavior and subsequent animal performance of 14-month-old heifers in response to multiple salt limited supplements while grazing Summer/Fall pasture over 2 consecutive years (73 heifers in Year 1 and 87 heifers in Year 2). Cattle were stratified by body weight (BW) and, within stratum, randomly assigned to one of three treatments in a randomized complete design: 1) Ad libitum access to salt-limited protein supplement only (30% crude protein, 25% NaCl); 2) Ad libitum access to only loose mineral salt (25% NaCl); and 3) Ad libitum access to both the protein and loose mineral supplement. Both supplements were offered in a Smartfeed Pro Trailer (C-Lock Inc, Rapid City, SD) that measured individual animal intake over the 84-day grazing period. Body weight and condition were recorded following a 16 hour shrink on days -0, -28, -56, and -84. There was no treatment effect on animal average daily gain (P > 0.58) and body condition score change (P > 0.81), averaging 0.76 kg/d. and 0.13 BCS. All metrics of protein and mineral intake displayed a three-way interaction between year, period, and treatment (P < 0.01). In year one, daily protein intake increased from 0.39 kg/d in period 1 to 1.83 kg/d in period 3 (P < 0.01). In year 2, daily protein intake increased from 0.34 kg/d in period 1 to 0.55 kg/d in period 3 (P < 0.01). Within each period of each year, there were no differences between treatments in terms of protein supplement intake. In period 1 of year 1, mineral intake was greater for animals with access to both supplements compared to heifers that had access to only mineral (p < 0.01; 110 g/day versus 17 g/day, respectively). However, mineral intake was lower in periods 2 and 3 for heifers that had access to both supplements (P < 0.01; 26 g/day vs 78 g/day, respectively). In year 2, mineral intake by heifers with access to both supplements was less for all three periods (63 g/day) than heifers that had access to mineral alone (12 g/day; P < 0.01). These results indicate that offering a salt-limited protein supplement and loose mineral salt may influence intake behavior of mineral supplement. This is an important implication for grazing systems that use self-fed, salt-limited supplements, especially if saline soils and water are a concern.
